title: The whole story in chapter one
hook: Narada tells the whole Ramayana in one chapter, ending and all, and people still come back to it
carry: the Ramayana is read for dharma, not suspense
tomorrow: who was the poet from the anthill?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Narada, and Valmiki's question. Is anyone good all the way through? Narada said: I know one. Rama.
screen: `IS ANYONE GOOD ALL THE WAY THROUGH?`

segments.voice: Episode one of a long series. A character turns to the camera and tells you everything: who leaves home, who gets taken, who wins the war, how it ends. Spoilers, all of them, in the first ten minutes. That's chapter one of the Ramayana. Narada answers Valmiki's question with the entire story, start to finish, in about a hundred verses. And people have kept reading the hundreds of chapters that follow anyway.
screen: `EPISODE ONE TELLS YOU EVERYTHING.` → `A HUNDRED VERSES, START TO FINISH.` → `AND PEOPLE KEEP READING.`

segments.voice: Here's Narada's outline. Rama, the eldest son of King Dasharatha, deeply loved, is about to be made heir. But a queen, Kaikeyi, calls in two promises the king once made her: exile for Rama, the throne for her own son Bharata. Rama goes to the forest without a word of protest, and his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana go with him. The king dies of grief. Bharata refuses the throne and rules only in Rama's name. In the forest, the demon king Ravana carries Sita off. Rama searches, befriends the monkey king Sugriva, and Hanuman leaps the ocean to find her in Lanka. A bridge is built, a war is fought, Ravana falls, and Rama comes home to rule. The whole epic, in a single chapter. It's known as the short Ramayana. Why give it all away? Remember Valmiki's question: is anyone good all the way through? The Ramayana isn't asking what happens. It's asking how to live. How a son keeps his father's word. How a brother says no to a crown that isn't his. How a wife holds firm. Hindus call that dharma: the right way to act, the order that holds a life and a world together. Many Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama, the best of people, who never steps outside dharma's bounds. So the story is built for return, not suspense. Grandparents tell it to children who already know it. At Ramlila plays each autumn, the audience knows the ending before the curtain rises. You don't come back to find out who wins. You come back to watch how Rama answers, and to ask how you would. Narada even ends with a promise: whoever reads this story of Rama is blessed by it.
screen: `EXILE, FOREST, ABDUCTION, WAR, RETURN.` · `THE WHOLE EPIC IN ONE CHAPTER.` · `NOT WHAT HAPPENS, BUT HOW TO LIVE.` · `DHARMA: THE RIGHT WAY TO ACT.` · then, large: `READ FOR DHARMA, NOT SUSPENSE.`

segments.voice: Pick one person from Narada's outline: Rama walking to the forest without protest, or Bharata saying no to a crown. Stay with that one choice for the sit. When your mind wanders, come back to the moment they chose. If you pray, let the name Rama ride softly on each out-breath.
Samkshepa, the short form. Narada's answer to Valmiki tells the whole Ramayana in one chapter, so the epic begins already knowing its ending.
Your line: the Ramayana is read for dharma, not suspense. You already know the ending; you come back to learn how to live. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Across India and beyond, the Ramayana is retold every year: recited in homes and temples, sung, and acted in village Ramlila performances in the autumn season, by audiences who already know the story.

notes: The summary's details (Kaikeyi's two boons, Sugriva, Hanuman, the bridge, Rama's reign without grief or early death) paraphrased from Bala Kanda 1; confirm which details Narada actually includes.
'About a hundred verses' and 'five hundred chapters' follow the traditional counts (sarga 1; Bala Kanda 4 speaks of five hundred sargas). Confirm.
'For well over a thousand years' is deliberately cautious; dating of the epic is debated.
